title: Detection of Search Engines
summary: This strategy detects the use of search engines to collect information about the victim, ATT&CK sub technique T1593.002. The adversary runs ordinary web searches that combine the organisation name with terms for exposed documents, credentials, login pages, vendor products and staff, looking for anything the organisation published by mistake or revealed unintentionally. Because the searches go to public search engines, the only internal evidence is web egress telemetry: secure web gateway logs that retain the query string, transport layer security metadata that shows only the destination, and recursive domain name system resolver logs that show which search or translation service host was resolved. Detection is a correlation between a destination that is a search engine and a query term drawn from the organisation's own naming, weighted by the identity and address behind the request. The technique is deliberately unremarkable, so the signal is weak and the strategy depends entirely on context and volume. It fails because almost every employee searches the web all day, because encrypted query strings hide the search terms when the proxy does not perform content inspection, and because an adversary working from outside your network never appears in this telemetry at all.

beginner.definition: Almost everyone uses a search engine every day, so this sounds impossible to detect. The clue is not the search itself but what is searched. This detection looks for web searches that pair your company name with sensitive words, such as password, database or login. It reports who searched and from where.
beginner.whyItMatters: People are the weakest link. Search engines are how attackers study them. A search can reveal a public document with a hidden account. It can also show an old test system that is still reachable. A job advert may list every tool the company runs. This is free research with no footprint on your network. Recording searches that mention your own organisation gives you a cheap early warning. It also shows you what is easy to find about you.
howItWorks: Your secure web gateway writes a log line for each web request, including the search words if it inspects the address.
The rule keeps requests that go to search engines.
It checks whether the address also contains one of your protected terms, such as your domain or a product name.
It records the account, the device and the address that made the request.
Normal employee searching is filtered out by learning the usual volume and the usual accounts.
Requests that fall outside the normal pattern are grouped and sent as a low priority lead.
beginner.example: Imagine a library with a sign in sheet at the door. Thousands of people come in each day to read, and nobody watches them. The librarian notices one visitor. This person only ever uses the reference desk to ask about one company. They ask about its address and its managers. They ask about its suppliers and its computer systems. Every question is allowed and nothing is broken. After the fifth visit, the librarian makes a note. This detection is that note. The searching is normal, the focus is not.
takeaways: The behaviour is normal, so you must make the rule about your own names, not about searching.
Encrypted search terms limit this detection, so record what your tooling can actually see.
The real benefit is discovery: these alerts show you what is already easy to find about your company.

objectives: Explain how search engine queries are used to collect information about an organisation
Identify the egress telemetry that can retain search query strings and destinations
Build a protected term list from organisation names, domains and product names
Establish a baseline of normal employee search volume to keep the rule usable
Recognise the telemetry gaps created by encrypted query strings and inspection limits
Use the findings to review what sensitive material is publicly discoverable
dataSources: Secure web gateway logs retaining the full requested uniform resource locator including the search query string
Recursive domain name system resolver logs showing lookups for search engine and web translation service domains
Transport layer security metadata records showing destination host names where full uniform resource locators are not available
Identity provider sign in records used to attribute queries to an account and device
Search engine alerting or brand monitoring feeds that record public queries containing the organisation name
logic: The detection pairs a search engine destination with a query that contains one of the organisation's protected terms. The destination is identified from the requested host or the uniform resource locator pattern, and the protected term list is built from company names, registered domains, product names and internal project names. The fields that must be correlated are the destination host, the query string, the authenticated account or absence of authentication, the source address, and the count of matching queries for that actor per day. The malicious case is an unauthenticated or unknown actor, a source address outside the corporate ranges, or a short window in which one actor runs many queries that each combine a protected term with a sensitive suffix such as password, backup, login or virtual private network. The benign case is an ordinary employee searching for public information, a marketing or public relations account running brand checks, or a threat intelligence analyst reviewing exposure, all of which stay inside the normal volume and account baseline.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Organisation Terms Searched On Search Engine From Odd Source
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: proxy
# detection:
#   selection_engine:
#     url|contains:
#       - 'google.com/search'
#       - 'bing.com/search'
#   selection_terms:
#     url|contains:
#       - 'acme-corp'
#       - 'project-atlas'
#   filter_expected:
#     group|contains:
#       - 'marketing'
#   filter_baseline:
#     query_count|lt: 25
#   condition: selection_engine and selection_terms and not filter_expected and not filter_baseline
# level: low
falsePositives: Recruitment, marketing and public relations staff searching for the company name as part of monitoring its public reputation
Employees searching for directions, contact details or a colleague's public profile before a meeting
Phishing simulation and security awareness campaigns in which the security team searches for public exposure of the organisation
Threat intelligence and brand protection services that query search engines for organisation names on a schedule
tuningNotes: Keep the protected term list short, distinctive and maintained with the marketing team, because a generic company name appears in unrelated searches and will bury the real leads. Filter by identity group and by a daily query count rather than by source address, since staff work remotely, and add a filter for the security and brand monitoring accounts. Set the first release to alert only on queries that combine a protected term with a sensitive suffix, which greatly reduces volume at the cost of missing plain name searches. Where the gateway cannot see query strings because of encryption, do not lower the bar to destination only, because that produces pure noise; instead note the coverage gap and consider search engine brand monitoring feeds as a compensating source.
